name: Starting an AI Consulting Business
objectives: Given the industries and businesses you know, write a one-sentence consulting offer for a specific type of client, naming who you help, the result and how
Given one business willing to try your help, plan a pilot with one measurable result and before-and-after numbers, with the client's written permission before any result is shared

Given your offer and hourly costs, create three service packages with deliverables, time, client inputs and prices, with the hourly math checked in a spreadsheet, including checking and follow-up time
Given your network and niche, plan outreach to ten possible clients and outline a short talk for owners, with personal messages that include your address and an opt-out
Given a 10-question audit questionnaire and one business owner, run an AI audit and recommend the top three AI uses, scoring ideas on time saved, cost, ease and risk, with a safeguard for each
For the business you audited, write a one-page proposal and your client data rules, with the client's situation in their own words and data deleted or returned at the end

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Choosing your niche and offer
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a one-sentence offer for a specific type of client.
This lesson builds toward: Given the industries and businesses you know, you will write a one-sentence consulting offer for a specific type of client, naming who you help, the result and how.
"I help businesses with AI" is hard to sell. "I help independent restaurants save 5 hours a week on ordering, scheduling and social media with simple AI tools" is easy to understand and easy to refer.
Choose a niche where you already have experience or contacts: an industry you worked in, a community you belong to, or a type of organization (salons, churches, contractors, clinics' front offices, nonprofits). Your past experience is your advantage over general tech people.
Ask AI to help: "I worked 8 years in [field]. List the repeated tasks small businesses in this field do that AI tools could speed up." Then write your offer: who you help, what result, and how.
Step by step:
- List industries or communities you know well.
- Ask AI for repeated tasks in those fields that AI could speed up.
- Pick one niche.
- Write your offer: who you help, what result, how.
Words to know:
- Consultant: an expert who advises a business and helps it make changes.
- Niche: a specific type of client you focus on.
- Offer: a clear statement of who you help, the result and how.
Try it now: Choose your niche with AI's help and write your one-sentence offer: who, what result, how.
You can now describe a focused AI consulting offer that clients understand quickly.

check.q: What is a niche in consulting?
options: A specific type of client you focus on
check.why: A niche lets you understand clients' problems deeply.

check.q: Your offer reads "I help businesses with AI". What do you do?
options: Name who you help, the result and how
Add a list of every AI tool
check.why: A strong offer is specific so clients understand it quickly.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Building proof with a pilot
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Plan a small pilot project that gives you a real result to show.
This lesson builds toward: Given one business willing to try your help, you will plan a pilot with one measurable result and before-and-after numbers, with the client's written permission before any result is shared.
Clients want proof you can help. If you are new, run a pilot: a small, short project for one business (a friend's shop, a local nonprofit) at a low or no fee, in exchange for permission to share the results and a testimonial.
Pick a pilot with a measurable result: "Set up AI reply templates and cut email time from 6 to 3 hours a week." Measure before and after.
Write it up as a short case study: the problem, what you did, the result in numbers, and a quote from the owner. Get written permission before sharing, and remove anything private. Never make up results or testimonials.
Step by step:
- Find one business willing to try a pilot.
- Agree on one measurable result.
- Measure before you start.
- Do the work and measure after.
- Write a short case study with permission.
Words to know:
- Pilot: a small trial project to show something works.
- Case study: a short story of a real project: problem, work, result.
- Testimonial: a client's statement about your work, used with their permission.
Try it now: Write a pilot plan: which business, one measurable result, how you will measure before and after, and what you ask in return.
You can now plan a pilot that turns into honest proof for your consulting business.

options: One result with before and after numbers
check.why: A measurable result turns a pilot into honest proof.

check.q: Your pilot saved the client 2 hours a week, not the 5 you hoped. What do you share?
options: The real result, with the client's permission
check.why: Never invent results; share only what really happened.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Packaging and pricing your services
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Create three service packages with clear deliverables and prices.
This lesson builds toward: Given your offer and hourly costs, you will create three service packages with deliverables, time, client inputs and prices, with the hourly math checked in a spreadsheet, including checking and follow-up time.
Packages are easier to buy than open-ended hours. A common set: an AI Audit (review the business and recommend the top three AI uses), an AI Setup (set up tools, templates and simple automations), and AI Training (teach the owner and staff, with written guides). Some consultants add a monthly support plan.
For each package write: what the client gets, how long it takes, what you need from them, and the price. Price from value and from your time: estimate your hours, include time for checking and follow-up, and compare with what similar local services charge.
Get an EIN from the IRS if you need one (the IRS says it is free and warns about sites that charge). As a self-employed person you generally pay self-employment tax and may need quarterly estimated taxes; see irs.gov and talk to an accountant.
Step by step:
- Write three packages: Audit, Setup, Training.
- For each: deliverables, time, what you need from the client, price.
- Estimate your hours including checking and follow-up.
- Compare with local rates and check your math.
- Look up tax basics on irs.gov and ask an accountant.
Words to know:
- Package: a defined service with set deliverables and a set price.
- Retainer: a monthly fee for ongoing help.
- EIN: Employer Identification Number: a free federal tax ID for a business from the IRS.
Official sources:
- IRS: Get an Employer Identification Number
- IRS: Self-Employed Individuals Tax Center
Try it now: Write your three packages with deliverables, time, client inputs and a price for each, and check your hourly math in a spreadsheet.
You can now package and price AI consulting services clearly.

check.q: Why sell packages instead of open-ended hours?
options: They are easier for clients to understand and buy
They remove the need for deliverables
check.why: Clear packages make buying simple for clients.

check.q: Your package price leaves no time for follow-up questions. What do you do?
options: Add follow-up time to your hours and reset the price
Charge extra later without telling the client
check.why: Pricing must include checking and follow-up time.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Finding your first clients
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Plan outreach to your first ten possible clients.
This lesson builds toward: Given your network and niche, you will plan outreach to ten possible clients and outline a short talk for owners, with personal messages that include your address and an opt-out.
Your first clients usually come from people who already know you: past co-workers, local business groups, your church or community, and referrals from your pilot. A free short talk or workshop ("5 ways AI can save your salon time") is a strong way to meet owners.
Write personal messages, not mass emails. AI can draft them: "Write a 70-word message to a salon owner I met at a chamber event, offering a free 20-minute AI check-up. Friendly, no hype." Add a real detail.
If you email people for business, follow CAN-SPAM basics: honest From and subject lines, your physical address and a clear opt-out, honored within 10 business days. Do not promise results you cannot prove.
Step by step:
- List ten owners or organizations in your niche you can reach.
- Plan one free talk or workshop.
- Draft personal messages with AI and add a real detail to each.
- Include your address and an opt-out in business emails.
- Track who you contacted and their reply.
Words to know:
- Referral: a recommendation from someone who knows your work.
- Workshop: a short session where you teach a group something useful.
Official sources:
- FTC: CAN-SPAM Act Compliance Guide for Business
Try it now: List ten possible clients, write three personal outreach messages with AI's help, and outline a 20-minute talk you could give to owners in your niche.
You can now reach your first clients through people you know, talks and honest outreach.

check.q: Where do first consulting clients usually come from?
options: People who already know you and referrals
check.why: Your network and referrals trust you first.

check.q: AI drafts an outreach email with no address or opt-out. What do you do?
options: Send it to a bought list
Add your physical address and an opt-out line
check.why: Business outreach emails must include an address and an opt-out.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Running an AI audit
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Interview a business owner and recommend their top three AI uses.
This lesson builds toward: Given a 10-question audit questionnaire and one business owner, you will run an AI audit and recommend the top three AI uses, scoring ideas on time saved, cost, ease and risk, with a safeguard for each.
An AI audit is a structured look at how a business works and where AI could help. Use a short questionnaire: What tasks take the most time each week? What do customers ask most? Where do mistakes happen? What tools do you already use? What worries you about AI?
From the answers, score each possible AI use on time saved, cost, ease and risk. AI can help you sort and score (with the business's name and private details removed), but your judgment matters most. Pick the top three: quick wins first.
Include risks and safeguards for each recommendation: who checks AI output, what data must stay out of AI tools, and anything that needs a lawyer or accountant. Honest limits make clients trust you more.
Step by step:
- Use a 10-question audit questionnaire with the owner.
- List every possible AI use you heard.
- Score each on time saved, cost, ease and risk.
- Pick the top three, quick wins first.
- Add a safeguard for each: human check, data rule, expert if needed.
Words to know:
- AI audit: a structured review of a business to find where AI can help safely.
- Quick win: a change that is easy to make and helps right away.
- Safeguard: a step that prevents harm, like a human check.
Try it now: Write your 10-question audit questionnaire and run it with one real business owner (or a friend acting as one). Score the ideas and write the top three with safeguards.
You can now run an AI audit and give a business three safe, practical recommendations.

check.q: Which audit recommendations should come first?
options: Quick wins that are easy and help right away
check.why: Quick wins build trust and show value early.

check.q: You want AI to help sort your audit notes. What do you do first?
options: Remove the business's name and private details
check.why: Client details stay out of AI tools.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Proposals, agreements and client data
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a one-page proposal and your rules for handling client data.
This lesson builds toward: For the business you audited, you will write a one-page proposal and your client data rules, with the client's situation in their own words and data deleted or returned at the end.
A proposal turns your audit into a decision. One page: the client's situation in their words, the three recommendations, the package you suggest, what you will deliver and when, the price, and what you need from them. AI can draft it from your notes; edit it so every promise is one you can keep.
Get a written agreement before starting paid work: scope, price, payment terms, timeline, who owns what you create, and confidentiality. Templates exist, but have a lawyer review yours.
Write client data rules and follow them: never put a client's customer lists, financial records, passwords or private information into AI tools without their written permission and a tool whose data terms fit; use their accounts, not yours, for tools that hold their data; and delete or return their data when the project ends. The FTC's guide on protecting personal information is a good base.
Step by step:
- Draft a one-page proposal from your audit notes with AI.
- Check every promise and price.
- Prepare a written agreement and have a lawyer review it.
- Write your client data rules.
- Share the rules with clients before you start.
Words to know:
- Proposal: a short document offering specific work at a specific price.
- Confidentiality: keeping a client's information private.
- Scope: exactly what work is included.
Official sources:
- FTC: Protecting Personal Information, A Guide for Business
Try it now: Final task: write the one-page proposal for the business you audited and your client data rules, then assemble your consulting starter kit: offer, packages, questionnaire, audit results, proposal and data rules.
You can now win and serve AI consulting clients with clear proposals, agreements and data rules.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Niche and offer The offer is vague or has no clear client. One sentence naming who, the result and how. Uses words that clients in the niche actually use. Service packages Fewer than three packages, or prices with no math behind them. Three packages with deliverables, time, client inputs and prices, math checked. Includes checking and follow-up time and explains the value to the client. AI audit No questionnaire, or recommendations without scores or safeguards. 10-question questionnaire, one real audit, top three uses scored with safeguards. Recommendations start with quick wins and show expected time saved. Proposal The proposal is generic or missing scope or price. One page with the client's situation in their words, scope, price and timeline. Includes a measurable result and how it will be checked. Client data rules No written rules, or private details went into AI. Written rules: permission, client's own accounts, data deleted or returned at the end. Also covers which AI tools may hold client data and checking their terms. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What does a written consulting agreement cover?
options: Scope, price, payment, timeline, ownership and confidentiality

check.q: The project is over and you still hold the client's files. What do you do?
options: Delete or return them as your data rules say
check.why: Client data should be deleted or returned at the end of a project.
